children.title: Abstract
children.body: We study the Lyapunov exponent in quantum field theories with spacetime-independent disorder interactions. Generically can only be computed at isolated points in parameter space, and little is known about the way in which chaos grows as we deform the theory away from weak coupling. In this paper we describe families of theories in which the disorder coupling is an exactly marginal deformation, allowing us to follow from weak to strong coupling. We find surprising behaviors in some cases, including a discontinuous transition into chaos. We also derive self-consistency equations for the two- and four-point functions for products of nontrivial CFTs deformed by disorder at leading order in .

Disordered theories display an interesting range of physical phenomena. Disorder appears in many experimental setups, but it has also found theoretical applications. An especially interesting disordered theory is the SYK model [1, 2]. The SYK model is defined as taking free fermions and deforming them by a random interaction:

with a random variable drawn from a Gaussian distribution with zero mean and variance (with no sum over repeated indices).

These are obtained by taking free fields (which can be fermions, bosons or superfields in any dimension) and coupling them using the spacetime-independent disorder interaction1

where are random variables taken from a Gaussian distribution with zero mean, and the disorder interaction can be either a potential or a superpotential term. For example, taking to be a free fermion in d and interpreting (1.2) as the Hamiltonian, one obtains the SYK model. Similarly, taking to be a d free chiral superfield and interpreting (1.2) as a superpotential, one obtains the MSW model [3]. There are also generalizations to and in quantum mechanics [4], d [5], d [6], and d [7], among others.

children.body: The disorder allows for some exact computations in these theories in the IR at leading order in , assuming that they flow to a scale-invariant fixed point [1, 8, 9]. In particular, one can write down and solve a Schwinger-Dyson equation for the 2-point function, and solve it using a conformal ansatz. In addition, the diagrams contributing to the four-point function of the theory obey an iterative ladder structure, and so they can be formally resummed, allowing for computation of the full four-point function of the theory. Higher-order correlators can also be computed [10].

gist.html: Disorder makes these models solvable at large $N$: a Schwinger–Dyson equation for two points, resummable ladders for four.

children.title: Disorder averaging and the SYK model
children.body: In the SYK model, a disorder model, each fermion interacts with all others through couplings that are random and of size $1/N^{(q-1)/2}$. Averaging over the couplings pairs them up, and at large $N$ only a special class of Feynman diagrams survives: the melons, in which every propagator is dressed by the same self-energy. The full propagator then obeys a closed Schwinger–Dyson equation, $\Sigma=J^2G^{q-1}$ together with $G=1/(G_0^{-1}-\Sigma)$. At strong coupling the free term $G_0^{-1}$ can be dropped, the equation becomes scale invariant, and a power-law ansatz solves it, with dimension $1/q$. The four-point function at order $1/N$ is a sum of ladders built from the same melons, summed through the eigenvalues of one kernel. The paper asks how much of this structure survives when the free fermions are replaced by an interacting core CFT.

In this paper we consider a more general construction. Consider a CFT in d dimensions, which contains a primary operator of dimension . We will study copies of this core CFT, deformed by a disorder interaction:

(1.3)

where are again Gaussian random variables with variance , and the disordered interaction term can be interpreted as a potential or a superpotential. These theories can be studied in conformal perturbation theory in . We will call such theories disordered CFTs. As an example, in this notation we refer to SYK-like models as disordered free fields, since the core CFT is a free field theory.

gist.html: Defines disordered CFTs: $N$ copies of any core CFT, coupled through a random product of one operator.

children.body: As discussed above, for disordered free fields there is a simple structure to the diagrammatic contributions to the two- and four-point functions at leading order in . Surprisingly, we will be able to show that a similar structure exists also for the computations of two- and four-point functions in general disordered CFTs. For example, one can still write down a Schwinger-Dyson equation for the exact two-point function (see figure 6). In addition, the contributions to the four-point function still exhibit an iterative ladder structure (see figure 8), which can be formally resummed. We will write down explicitly the corresponding equations from which the two- and four-point functions can be extracted for general disordered CFTs.

gist.html: Surprisingly, the Schwinger–Dyson equation and the ladder structure of four-point functions survive for interacting core CFTs.

children.body: Unfortunately, since interacting CFTs are much more complicated than free theories, the corresponding equations one must solve in order to find the exact two- and four-point functions are much more complicated as well. In particular, in order to solve the equations we must know all -point functions of the CFTs. These computations are thus practically possible only in specific CFTs. In this paper we will be able to use the equations to study disordered generalized free fields and a disordered minimal model.

gist.html: The equations need every correlator of the core CFT, so they are solved only for special examples.

children.body: Although the generalized equations we will write down for the two- and four-point functions for disordered CFTs are complicated, they still allow us to study a new phenomenon. It is common in the literature to make the disorder deformation relevant, so that the theory flows to some fixed point in the IR. One can also try to use a disorder deformation that is classically marginal for disordered free fields, but these deformations are usually marginally irrelevant (see e.g. [11]). On the other hand, around nontrivial CFTs there is the possibility that these deformations are exactly marginal. In this paper we will mainly focus on exactly marginal deformations, at least at leading order in . In particular, this means that it is not necessary to take in order to find a fixed point; instead, the values of should parametrize a line of (disordered) fixed points.

gist.html: Around interacting CFTs disorder can be exactly marginal, unlike around free fields, giving a line of disordered fixed points.

children.body: The existence of a line of fixed points allows one to ask questions about the -dependence of observables in the theory, rather than just the large- (or IR) behavior as in disordered free fields. Famously, this chaos exponent is bounded from above [14], with the inverse temperature. Since we will be working around scale-invariant theories, will be the only scale in the problem and so we will set in the following, so that the bound reads .

children.title: Out-of-time-order correlators and the bound on chaos
children.body: In classical chaos, nearby trajectories separate as $e^{\lambda t}$. The quantum analogue compares a perturbation $W$ applied at time $t$ with a probe $V$ at time zero, through the squared commutator $\langle[W(t),V]^2\rangle$. Expanded, it contains correlators whose operators are not time ordered, hence the name out-of-time-order correlators. In large-$N$ systems the squared commutator starts at order $1/N$ and grows as $e^{\lambda_Lt}/N$, until it becomes of order one at the scrambling time, about $\lambda_L^{-1}\log N$. Maldacena, Shenker and Stanford proved that in a thermal state $\lambda_L\le2\pi/\beta$. The bound is saturated by black holes in Einstein gravity and by the SYK model at strong coupling, while weakly coupled theories have small $\lambda_L$. The paper follows $\lambda_L$ between these two ends along a line of conformal theories.

Usually, computing the chaos exponent requires the theory to be scale invariant, since this simplifies the computation immensely. As a result, is known mostly for some isolated CFTs. However, the structure described above allows us to compute the chaos exponent as a function of the continuous disorder parameter . We will thus be able to follow from , where the theory consists of a product of decoupled CFTs, to , where the theory usually coincides with some SYK-like fixed point. We expect there to be very low chaos at and large chaos at , and we would like to study how chaos emerges in the theory. For some previous discussions of quantum chaos at weak coupling which are similar to the discussion here, see [15, 16, 17, 18, 8, 6] and references therein, and specifically [19, 20] which discussed chaos on a line of fixed points in a non-Lorentz-invariant theory.

gist.html: So $\lambda_L$ can be followed from decoupled CFTs at $J=0$ to an SYK-like point at large $J$.

children.body: The question of how chaos appears following a small deformation of a non-chaotic theory is an extremely complicated one, even in classical systems. Classically, there are diverse types of behaviors that different systems can display, leading to a large range of interesting physical phenomena to study. Specifically, some interesting behavior occurs when one deforms an integrable system away from integrability. An important result in this context is the KAM theorem, which discusses the breakdown of integrability under a small deformation for non-degenerate integrable systems with a finite number of degrees of freedom. Schematically, the KAM theorem states that such systems which are slightly deformed away from integrability still retain a large part of their integrable structure. As a result, a “large” deformation away from integrability is required in order to find chaos. The fact that deformations away from integrability retain some integrable structure seems to be more robust than the range implied by the KAM theorem; another example of this behavior beyond the scope of the KAM theorem is the Fermi-Pasta-Ulam-Tsingou problem.

gist.html: Classically, the KAM theorem says nearly integrable systems keep much of their structure, so chaos needs a large deformation.

children.title: Integrable systems, invariant tori and the KAM theorem
children.body: A classical integrable system with $n$ degrees of freedom has $n$ conserved quantities, and its motion winds around $n$-dimensional invariant tori in phase space with fixed frequencies; nothing is chaotic. The Kolmogorov–Arnold–Moser theorem asks what a small perturbation does. If the unperturbed frequencies change with the tori (non-degeneracy), most tori, those whose frequency ratios are far enough from rational, survive, only deformed; the measure of destroyed tori goes to zero with the perturbation. Chaos appears first in thin layers around the destroyed resonant tori, and widespread chaos requires a finite perturbation. The theorem needs finitely many degrees of freedom, and its bounds on the perturbation are often very small; the Fermi–Pasta–Ulam–Tsingou chain shows regular behaviour persisting beyond them. The paper's discontinuous onset of quantum chaos is its loose analogue.

We will find that disordered quantum systems also display different types of behaviors when deformed away from a non-chaotic point. In particular, we will find two types of behavior for the chaos exponent , shown in figure 1.

gist.html: Disordered quantum systems also show different kinds of onset of chaos as they are deformed from a non-chaotic point.

children.title: (1a)

gist.html: Two onsets of chaos: $\lambda_L$ growing from $J=0$ (continuous), or zero until a critical $J_c$ (discontinuous).

children.body: Schematically, we find that disordered CFTs can either have a continuous or a discontinuous transition into chaos. The discontinuous transition into chaos is an extremely interesting result, and parallels the behavior one might expect from systems which fall under the classes described in KAM theory, but the analogy is very far from being precise. The KAM theorem was an exciting breakthrough in the study of the onset of classical chaos, and we hope that a similar breakthrough may appear in the study of the onset of quantum chaos.

gist.html: The discontinuous transition loosely parallels KAM theory, though the analogy is far from precise.

children.body: The rest of this paper is organized as follows. In section 2, we discuss generalities of disordered CFTs at large . We write down the self-consistency equations for the two- and four-point functions, and discuss the computation of the chaos exponent. In section 3 we define the main classes of theories we will be interested in, where the disorder coupling is exactly marginal. In section 4 we discuss the first class of theories, the disordered generalized free fields, and we compute the chaos exponent as a function of for them. In section 5 we discuss the second class of theories, the disordered minimal models, and we find the chaos exponent in the limit for the simplest minimal model. We discuss our results and some future directions in section 6.

We now summarize the main results of this paper. There are two main results:

  1. First, we discuss the two- and four-point functions of general disordered CFTs. For the two-point function, we write down a self-consistency equation for the exact propagator (figure 6), which generalizes the standard Schwinger-Dyson equations of disordered free fields. We then show that the contributions to the four-point function have an iterative ladder structure (figure 8), again imitating the case for disordered free fields. In both cases the structure is much more complicated in a general CFT compared to a free theory, but it allows for a perturbative expansion in the disorder parameter .

  2. Second, we discuss chaos in the case where the disorder parameter is an exactly marginal deformation (at least at leading order in ). We show that the OTOC also obeys a ladder structure, which allows for a computation of the chaos exponent in the case where is exactly marginal. We perform this computation in two classes of examples:

    1. Disordered generalized free fields: we discuss generalized free fermions in d (following [21]) and SUSY generalized free chiral superfields in d. In both cases is exactly marginal at leading order in . We find that in this class of models there is a discontinuous transition into chaos as in figure 1b, so that the chaos exponent vanishes for couplings for some finite critical coupling , before rising as we raise above . See figure 11 for the explicit result for the d case and figure 12 for the d case. Specifically, the chaos exponent read off from the ladder structure appears to be negative for , but as we explain this just signals a breakdown of some assumptions which are usually made in the computation of the chaos exponent, and should be interpreted as having for .

    2. Disordered SUSY minimal models: we discuss copies of the minimal models coupled by disorder. The computation of is difficult in general, and so we focus on the particularly simple case of , where the theory has central charge and so it reduces to that of a free compact boson. This allows us to compute all possible correlators of the relevant chiral superfields, and to compute the leading contribution to the chaos exponent at small . We find that there is a smooth transition into chaos in this case, as in figure 1a.

gist.html: Lists the results: general equations, a discontinuous onset for generalized free fields, a smooth one for the $A_2$ minimal model.

children.body: This paper is just a first step in the study of the onset of quantum chaos in disordered systems, and many open questions remain. In particular, we conjecture a continuity relation around equation (2.37), which relates the chaos exponent of disordered CFTs obtained via the retarded kernel in the limit to an exponent in a specific limit of a single core CFT. If this is a general result, then it would suffice to study a simple limit of a single copy of the core CFT in order to find whether the transition into chaos is continuous or discontinuous for the disordered CFTs. It would be very interesting to either prove this result or find a counter-example. Some additional particularly interesting open questions are discussed in the conclusions in section 6.

gist.html: Conjectures a continuity relation: the weak-coupling chaos exponent follows from a limit of a single core CFT.

children.body: Our results are also summarized in the companion paper [22].

gist.html: Two results: large-$N$ equations for any disordered CFT, and $\lambda_L(J)$ on exactly marginal lines, with two kinds of onset.

brief.html: The paper names two main results. First, the two-point function of any disordered CFT obeys a self-consistency equation and its four-point function a ladder, both usable order by order in $J$. Second, on exactly marginal lines the chaos exponent can be computed: disordered generalized free fields have no chaos below a finite $J_c$, while the simplest disordered supersymmetric minimal model enters chaos smoothly. A conjectured continuity relation would let one copy of the core CFT decide which kind of onset occurs.

gist.html: Exactly marginal disorder lets the chaos exponent be followed in coupling; chaos switches on continuously or discontinuously.

brief.html: Random couplings make SYK-like models solvable at large $N$; the paper asks whether the same works when the copies being coupled are interacting conformal theories, not free fields. Around such theories the disorder can be exactly marginal, so each coupling $J$ is itself a conformal theory, and the chaos exponent can be followed from decoupled copies at $J=0$ to strong coupling. Two kinds of onset appear: continuous, and discontinuous, with no chaos below a finite coupling, loosely as in the KAM theorem of classical mechanics.

In disordered free field theories defined in equation (1.2), the random interactions impose a specific structure on the perturbative expansion of some observables. This allows for a resummation of Feynman diagrams, and in some cases allows for an exact computation of some observables in the theory at large . In particular:

  • One can write down a Schwinger-Dyson equation for the two-point function of two ’s (which are the free fields at ). In the conformal limit , this can be solved exactly.

  • In addition, the contributions to the four-point function of ’s obey an iterative ladder structure, which can be resummed in principle.

  • Finally, the out-of-time-ordered four-point function (the OTOC) also has an iterative ladder structure, which can be used to extract the chaos exponent of the theory even without an explicit resummation.

children.body: Since the core CFT is no longer a free theory, we cannot use the self-consistency equations for the two-and four-point functions discussed above. However, we will show that in the more general case (2.1), it is still possible to perform some exact computations in these theories. Specifically, we will show that it is still possible to write down a Schwinger-Dyson (SD) equation for the two-point function, and that the four-point function and the OTOC still obey an iterative ladder structure, which allows one to extract the chaos exponent. We will eventually be interested only in deformations which are exactly marginal, but the self-consistency equations we write will be general. We comment that in general, further counter-terms are required to renormalize the theory, but we will assume that these either average to zero or are not required for the specific correlators we will study (indeed we will see that this is the case for the models discussed in this paper, at least to the order in we will work in).

children.title: Classically and exactly marginal deformations
children.body: Deforming a conformal field theory by $g\int d^dx\,\mathcal O$, with $\mathcal O$ of dimension exactly $d$, is classically marginal: $g$ is dimensionless. Quantum corrections decide whether it stays so. In conformal perturbation theory the beta function starts as $\beta_g\propto C_{\mathcal{OOO}}\,g^2$, with $C_{\mathcal{OOO}}$ the coefficient of $\mathcal O$ in its own operator product expansion. If it is non-zero, $g$ runs, and one sign makes the deformation marginally irrelevant: it dies away logarithmically at long distances, as many disorder couplings of free fields do. If the beta function vanishes to all orders, the deformation is exactly marginal and $g$ labels a family of conformal theories, a conformal manifold. Exactly marginal deformations are rare without supersymmetry. The paper uses them to keep every value of the disorder $J$ conformal.

brief.html: When the disorder is exactly marginal the theory is conformal at every $J$, so a conformal eigenfunction ansatz turns the retarded kernel into an eigenvalue $k_R(\lambda,J)$, and $\lambda_L(J)$ is its largest root of $k_R=1$. Because $k_R$ is of order $J^2$, the weak-coupling exponent sits where its integrals diverge, argued to be at the late-time exponent $\lambda_L^0$ of a single core CFT. gist.html: Around any core CFT, large-$N$ disorder still gives a Schwinger–Dyson equation and ladder sums for four-point functions and OTOCs.

brief.html: The structures that make SYK solvable survive when the free fields are replaced by any core CFT. Rewriting the averaged theory with bilocal fields $G$ and $\Sigma$, the core CFT enters only through a generating functional of its correlators, and the large-$N$ saddle gives a generalized Schwinger–Dyson equation. Fluctuations give a ladder for the four-point function, and its continuation a retarded ladder for the double commutator. On exactly marginal lines this yields $\lambda_L(J)$, and near $J=0$ it ties $\lambda_L$ to the late-time exponent of one copy.

children.body: We will discuss two main examples of disorder around generalized free fields (GFFs). One is the cSYK line of fixed points in quantum mechanics [21], and another is the d version of this line of fixed points. The RG flows for these theories are schematically shown in figure 10. In the figure, we have assumed that disordered GFFs at large reach the same fixed point as the corresponding disordered free fields at large . Intuitively, this is because the disorder interaction “dominates” at large , and so the original core CFT plays no role. Indeed, [21] found evidence for this result, and we will provide additional evidence here for both the QM model and the d model.

children.title: Generalized free fields
children.body: A free field of dimension $\Delta$ is generalized when $\Delta$ is not the free value, $(d-2)/2$ for a scalar in $d$ dimensions: its two-point function is the conformal $1/|x|^{2\Delta}$, and every higher correlator is the sum over Wick pairings of two-point functions. This defines a consistent conformal theory, but a non-local one: its quadratic action has the kernel $1/|x-y|^{2d-2\Delta}$ in place of a derivative, and it has no stress tensor. Generalized free fields appear as the large-$N$ limit of single-trace operators in holographic theories, and in quantum mechanics as fermions with a non-local kinetic term. Because their correlators are all known, a disordered theory built on them can be solved exactly, which is what the cSYK model of Gross and Rosenhaus does with fermions of dimension $1/q$.

children.body: We can now argue that each deformation is exactly marginal. First, since , the deformation is classically marginal. However, since the CFT at has no continuous non-R global symmetries, every classically marginal operator is exactly marginal [32, 33, 34].13 We thus learn that every realization of the model is conformal. Clearly we end up on the same conformal manifold as described in the UV description above.

gist.html: Without continuous non-R global symmetries every classically marginal coupling is exactly marginal, so every realization is conformal.

children.title: Exactly marginal couplings and broken global symmetry
children.body: In supersymmetric theories with four supercharges, such as $4$d $\mathcal N=1$ or $1+1$d $\mathcal N=(2,2)$, a classically marginal superpotential coupling can fail to be exactly marginal in one way only. If the coupling breaks a continuous global symmetry, the broken current is no longer conserved, and it combines with the marginal operator into a longer multiplet that is marginally irrelevant. Green, Komargodski, Seiberg, Tachikawa and Wecht (and earlier Kol) showed that the conformal manifold is the space of marginal couplings divided by the complexified global symmetry group. So if the undeformed theory has no continuous non-R global symmetry, there is nothing to break, and every classically marginal coupling is exactly marginal. The $N$ decoupled minimal models have no such symmetry, which is why every realization of the paper's random couplings is a conformal theory.
Summary

We have thus found that the disordered minimal models defined in (3.24) describe a conformal manifold. This model should be understood as deforming copies of the minimal model by a disorder superpotential. This conformal manifold is the same as the one expected to appear had we started in the UV from free fields and deformed by a similar superpotential.

gist.html: The disordered minimal models span the same conformal manifold as the UV description.

children.body: We emphasize that the disorder average is an average over CFTs, i.e. we have a CFT at every realization of the theory, as opposed to the disorder average in the standard SYK model. This is similar to other recent examples where averages were performed over CFTs, see e.g. [26, 27].

children.body: In this paper we discussed disorder around general CFTs, which allowed us to compute the chaos exponent as a function of a continuous parameter in some specific models. We started by writing down a set of self-consistency equations for the two- and four-point functions (and also the OTOC) for a general disordered CFT. We then discussed models in which the disorder parameter is exactly marginal (at least at leading order in ). In principle this allowed us to compute the chaos exponent for any value of the disorder parameter , and to follow the theory from weak to strong chaos. We managed to perform this analysis explicitly for disordered generalized free fields in d and d. In addition, we performed this analysis to leading order in in the disordered minimal model. For the disordered generalized free fields we found a discontinuous transition into chaos, while for the disordered minimal model we found a continuous transition.

gist.html: Recaps: general equations, exactly marginal models, a discontinuous onset for generalized free fields, continuous for $A_2$.

children.body: As discussed above, in principle the computation (at least at leading order in ) should be possible for all of the minimal models, since their four-point functions are known [36]. It would be interesting to see whether the transitions to chaos in the general case would be continuous or discontinuous. In particular, the case should be the next simplest case after , since it has central charge and is the free chiral superfield [36]. As a result, the computation should parallel the one done above for , since we can map components of chiral superfields to vertex operators or fermionic operators, whose correlators are known. Naive dimensional analysis seems to indicate that the chaos exponent is continuous in this case, but the analysis should be done more carefully.

gist.html: Other $A_{q-1}$ minimal models are computable; $q=4$, a free $\mathcal N=(1,1)$ superfield, looks continuous by naive dimensional analysis.

children.body: One can also extend this analysis to 2+1d. The Wess-Zumino models defined in equation (3.24) have an immediate generalization to 2+1d theories with SUSY. In this case, only the case is a relevant deformation from the UV free field theory. This model was studied in [7], but it would be interesting to study the properties of the conformal manifold as well. This would be a much more daunting task than the d theories discussed here, since the d versions correspond to a disorder deformation of very simple CFTs (the minimal models), while the d versions correspond to complicated CFTs.

gist.html: $2+1$d $\mathcal N=2$ versions exist but disorder much harder CFTs.

children.body: An interesting result that was argued for above is the continuity relation (2.37). As a reminder, the chaos exponent near can either be computed explicitly by computing the OTOC at (and the result is denoted ), or computing from the eigenvalue equation for the kernel and taking the limit . Then we argued that . In addition, we showed that this relation is true in the explicit examples studied in this paper in sections 4.3 and 5.2. It would be very interesting to understand whether this is a general result for disordered CFTs. If it is a general result, then in principle one could find whether the transition into chaos is continuous or discontinuous by performing a computation in a single copy of one core CFT (since computing requires knowing only one copy of the core CFT). Then it would be interesting to understand precisely what set of conditions a core CFT is required to obey in order for the transition into chaos to be continuous or discontinuous.

gist.html: Whether the continuity relation is general is open; if so, one core CFT decides continuous or discontinuous.

children.body: Assuming this continuity condition on the chaos exponent, there are now many additional examples where the transition into chaos would be discontinuous - the idea would be to consider a single core CFT, and find (see (2.36)). If the result is negative, then we expect a discontinuous transition into chaos, assuming that a conformal manifold can be constructed at leading order in as above. In particular, we expect that the non-SUSY minimal models will have a discontinuous transition using the results of [37], and that the d Ising model will have a discontinuous transition using the results of [38], if similar conformal manifolds exist.

gist.html: Assuming continuity, non-supersymmetric minimal models and the $2+1$d Ising model should have discontinuous onsets, if conformal manifolds exist.

children.body: An additional result is that the perturbative expansion for the chaos exponent was indeed consistent, which was nontrivial as explained in section 2.5.2. In particular, it is crucial that the integrals coming from higher-order corrections diverge at which obeys . Relatedly, one must show that equation (2.42) is obeyed. Indeed, once again we saw explicitly that this is obeyed in the specific examples discussed in this paper. It would be nice to prove this behavior for a general CFT.

gist.html: Higher orders were consistent in the examples; a general proof of the needed late-time behaviour is lacking.

children.body: Our self-consistency equations for the two- and four-point functions around a general disordered CFT can be useful outside of the scope of this paper. It would be interesting to see if there are additional core CFTs for which these equations can be solved exactly apart from free fields. This would be especially useful in cases where the disorder deformation is not exactly marginal, since then the equations would probably be solvable only in the limit where conformal invariance may be restored, and so perturbation theory in will not be useful. It would also be interesting to try to solve these equations in perturbation theory to high orders in in the case where the disorder is exactly marginal. Finally, more general correlators can also be computed for disordered free fields [10], and it would be interesting to see if this is the case also for general disordered CFTs.

gist.html: The self-consistency equations may help elsewhere, for instance high-order perturbation theory on marginal lines.

children.body: It would be interesting to understand the dependence of the chaos exponent on exactly marginal deformations also from a holographic perspective. In particular, [39] studied a symmetric orbifold of the SUSY minimal models of the type reviewed in section 3. These theories have a much smaller number of exactly marginal deformations, but far along the conformal manifold the authors found evidence for a (weakly curved) holographic dual. It would be interesting to try to apply the methods discussed above to these examples and study as function of the exactly marginal deformation. If the theory is indeed holographic far away on the conformal manifold, should reach its maximal value . It would be interesting to show this and to study small deviations away from maximal chaos.

gist.html: If symmetric orbifolds of minimal models are holographic far along their conformal manifold, $\lambda_L$ should reach 1 there.

children.body: Finally, it would be very interesting to compare our results with classical expectations for the onset of chaos. As discussed above, there are exact theorems which described the chaotic behavior of some models as they are deformed away from weak coupling, like the KAM theorem. There are incredibly useful tools in studying classical chaos, and hopefully a better understanding of the onset of quantum chaos will lead to similar tools.

gist.html: Hopes that understanding the quantum onset of chaos yields tools like those of classical chaos.
Two kinds of onset found; the continuity relation would let one core CFT decide which, in many more theories.

brief.html: Exactly marginal disorder let the chaos exponent be followed in coupling: generalized free fields enter chaos discontinuously, the $A_2$ minimal model continuously. If the continuity relation holds generally, one copy of a core CFT decides the onset; non-supersymmetric minimal models and the $2+1$d Ising model would then be discontinuous, if suitable conformal manifolds exist. Open: other minimal models, $2+1$d versions, and holographic conformal manifolds where $\lambda_L$ should reach its maximum.

children.body: In this section we study the minimal model corresponding to the superpotential , known as the minimal model. This minimal model has central charge , and so it should correspond to the theory of a free compact boson at some value of the compactification radius .

children.body: It is slightly subtle to find the precise theory which the model maps to in the IR. The reason is that we are interested only in correlation functions in the CFT, and there are a handful of theories which differ only by gaugings of some discrete symmetries, so that correlators are invariant (assuming the operators are invariant under the symmetry we are gauging). In particular, the bosonic theory has four values of the radius where it has enhanced SUSY, which are and their T-dual values (see e.g. [40]). Indeed, the two theories at are orbifolds of each other, and so correlation functions do not differ between them. It is thus not important which value of we choose for our purposes.

gist.html: Radii related by orbifolds share correlators, so the precise radius does not matter here.

children.body: However, this is not the end of the story. Our SUSY theory includes fermions, and so it requires a choice of spin structure, while the standard bosonic theory does not. Indeed, the theories at discussed above are theories with SUSY, but where has been gauged (as we will see later on). Instead, our SUSY theory should correspond to a “fermionic” theory, i.e. a theory with a choice of spin structure.17 We will assume that the fermions can be introduced by an “ungauging” procedure of , i.e. we will assume that there is some symmetry which upon gauging reintroduces the fermions.

gist.html: The supersymmetric theory needs a spin structure; the fermions are assumed restored by ungauging $(-1)^F$.

children.body: The bottom line is then that the theory with superpotential flows to an orbifold of the standard bosonic theory with . • Context The chaos exponent $\lambda_L$ measures quantum chaos; it is known mostly for isolated theories.
  • Result
    • Random couplings among many copies of some conformal theories keep them conformal at any strength (for some, only at large $N$), so $\lambda_L$ can be tracked.

brief.html:
The chaos exponent $\lambda_L$ measures how fast out-of-time-order correlators grow, and is bounded by $2\pi/\beta$. Computing it usually needs scale invariance, so it is known mostly at isolated conformal points, and little is known about how chaos grows as a theory moves away from weak coupling. The paper couples $N$ copies of a conformal theory by random couplings that are exactly marginal, so every coupling strength $J$ is conformal and $\lambda_L(J)$ can be followed from $J=0$ upwards. For disordered generalized free fields chaos appears only above a finite coupling, which the paper calls a discontinuous transition. For a disordered supersymmetric minimal model it should appear continuously from $J=0$. The first behaviour loosely parallels the KAM theorem of classical mechanics, though the analogy is far from precise.

In the SYK model, where the copies are free fermions, averaging over couplings makes the propagator obey a closed Schwinger–Dyson equation and the four-point function a sum of ladder diagrams. The paper shows that this survives for an interacting core CFT. Rewritten with bilocal fields $G$ and $\Sigma$, the theory sees the core CFT only through a generating functional of its correlators, and the large-$N$ saddle gives a generalized Schwinger–Dyson equation. Fluctuations about the saddle sum the four-point function as a ladder $F_0/(1-K)$, whose kernel is built from core correlators with their disconnected parts subtracted. Exact solutions need every correlator of the core CFT, but each order in $J$ needs only finitely many. The double commutator obeys the same ladder with a retarded kernel, so $\lambda_L$ is the largest growth rate whose eigenvalue $k_R$ equals one.

In cSYK, Gross and Rosenhaus's model of generalized free fermions of dimension $1/q$, the coupling is exactly marginal at leading order in $1/N$, and the propagator is SYK's times a function of $J$. A $1+1$d supersymmetric version behaves alike. Among $N$ copies of the $\mathcal N=(2,2)$ $A_{q-1}$ minimal model, every random coupling of $q$ chiral fields is exactly marginal, because the copies have no continuous non-R global symmetry; so each realization is conformal. The resulting conformal manifold has dimension about $N^q/q!$. With many flavours of minimal models, the theory reduces to the supersymmetric generalized free fields, which therefore have a conformal manifold even at finite $N$.

At $J=0$ the copies decouple, and the double commutator of one copy decays at late times with an exponent $\lambda_L^0$, expected to be non-positive. It describes the eventual decay, not chaos. Since the kernel's eigenvalue is of order $J^2$, a solution near $J=0$ sits where its integral diverges, which the paper argues happens from $\lambda=\lambda_L^0$ down. A toy model gives a double pole there and $\lambda_L=\lambda_L^0+O(J)$, so the paper conjectures the continuity relation $\lambda_L(J\to0^+)=\lambda_L^0$. A negative root of $k_R=1$ means no exponentially growing solution, so the paper reads it as no chaos. A negative $\lambda_L^0$ thus predicts chaos only above a finite coupling, and a vanishing one an onset from zero.

For cSYK the retarded kernel is SYK's rescaled, so $\lambda_L(J)$ is found at every $J$. It reaches the maximal value 1 at strong coupling, but below a critical $J_c$ the root is negative, tending to $-2\Delta$. So for every finite $q$, and in the $1+1$d version for every $\Delta>0$, there is no chaos below $J_c$. For the $A_2$ minimal model, a $c=1$ compact boson whose correlators are all known, the integrals diverge only for $\lambda\le0$ at every order. So $\lambda_L(J\to0^+)=0$, and the onset should be continuous. Computed directly, $\lambda_L^0$ is $-2\Delta$ and 0 in the two families, so the continuity relation holds in both.

The continuity relation is argued, not proved: where the integrals diverge is expected rather than shown in general. For the minimal model only $q=3$ and the leading order in $J$ are computed; that $\lambda_L$ then grows with $J$ is assumed, and the higher-order argument skips the Euclidean integrals. The bosonic part of the kernel is assumed to dominate, and cSYK's marginality is established only at leading order in $1/N$. If continuity holds generally, one copy of a core CFT decides the kind of onset. The paper then expects non-supersymmetric minimal models and the $2+1$d Ising model to enter chaos discontinuously, if suitable conformal manifolds exist.

defs.html: Couplings drawn at random from a probability distribution, with observables averaged over the draws. Here they are Gaussian, of zero mean and variance set by $J^2$, and constant in space and time. At leading order in $1/N$ averaging the correlators (quenched) or the partition function (annealed) gives the same results.

defs.html: A conformal theory whose correlators are all products of two-point functions, by Wick's theorem, as for a free field, but whose field may have any dimension $\Delta$. It is conformal but non-local, with no stress tensor; such fields arise, for instance, at large $N$.

at.quote: minimal model.

defs.html: Said of a deformation that keeps the theory conformal at every value of its coupling. A classically marginal one has dimension equal to the spacetime dimension, but quantum effects can make it marginally relevant or irrelevant; an exactly marginal one stays marginal, its coupling labelling a family of CFTs.

defs.html: A one-parameter family of conformal theories, here labelled by the disorder strength $J$: a one-dimensional conformal manifold. It runs from $N$ decoupled core CFTs at $J=0$ towards an SYK-like fixed point as $J\to\infty$, and the averaged correlators are conformal all along it.

defs.html: The rate $\lambda_L$ at which out-of-time-ordered correlators grow at late times, $\sim e^{\lambda_Lt}$, the quantum analogue of a Lyapunov exponent. It obeys $\lambda_L\le2\pi/\beta$; the paper sets $\beta=2\pi$, so the bound is $\lambda_L\le1$, and $\lambda_L=0$ means no chaos.

defs.html: An out-of-time-ordered correlator, whose operators are not ordered along one time direction. The paper uses the thermal average of two commutators $[\mathcal O_i,\mathcal O_j(t)]$, half a thermal circle apart, and calls this double commutator the OTOC too; its exponential growth defines the chaos exponent.

at.quote: an out-of-time-ordered correlator (OTOC)

defs.html: The Kolmogorov–Arnold–Moser theorem of classical mechanics: in a non-degenerate integrable system with finitely many degrees of freedom, most invariant tori survive a small enough perturbation, only deformed. So weakly perturbed systems stay largely regular, and widespread chaos needs a finite perturbation.

defs.html: A 1950s numerical experiment on a chain of masses joined by weakly nonlinear springs. Energy put into one mode was expected to spread over all modes, as chaos would require, but instead returned almost periodically: nonlinearity alone did not make the chain ergodic.

defs.html: The paper's name for an onset of chaos at a finite coupling: $\lambda_L$ is zero for all $J$ below a critical $J_c$ and positive above it. In the paper's figures $\lambda_L$ itself rises from zero at $J_c$; what is abrupt is that chaos needs a finite coupling.

at.quote: The discontinuous transition into chaos is an extremely interesting result

defs.html: The paper's name for an onset of chaos at zero coupling: $\lambda_L$ is positive for every $J>0$ and tends to zero as $J\to0$. The paper finds it, at leading order and assuming $\lambda_L$ grows with $J$, for the disordered $A_2$ minimal model.

at.quote: can either have a continuous or a discontinuous transition into chaos

defs.html: A free massless scalar in two dimensions whose values are periodic, $\phi\sim\phi+2\pi R$: the $c=1$ conformal theories, one for each radius $R$. Its correlators are products of vertex operators $e^{ik\phi}$, known exactly, and at special radii it has extra symmetry, including $\mathcal N=(2,2)$ supersymmetry.

at.quote: it reduces to that of a free compact boson

defs.html: The rung of the ladder for the double commutator, $K_R$: the four-point kernel continued to real time, with each new pair of points in the past of the previous one. Its eigenvalue $k_R(\lambda)$ on a mode growing as $e^{\lambda t}$ equals one at $\lambda=\lambda_L$.

at.quote: obtained via the retarded kernel

defs.html: The paper's conjecture $\lambda_L(J\to0^+)=\lambda_L^0$: the chaos exponent computed from the retarded kernel, as the coupling goes to zero, equals the exponent of the late-time decay of the double commutator in a single core CFT. It is argued generally and verified in the paper's examples.

at.quote: we conjecture a continuity relation

defs.html: A chaos exponent equal to its upper bound $2\pi/\beta$, which is 1 in the paper's units. Black holes in Einstein gravity and the strongly coupled SYK model saturate it; the disordered generalized free fields approach it at strong coupling.

at.quote: SYK has maximal chaos

defs.html: The paper's combinations of core-CFT correlators that enter its equations: the $n$-point function minus products of lower ones, removing what would give disconnected diagrams. They are written $n_s$ in the Schwinger–Dyson equation and $n_s'$, with different subtractions, in the four-point kernel.

at.quote: the “subtracted four-point function”

defs.html: The two vertical segments of the complex time contour used for the double commutator: excursions in real time to $it_1$ and to $\beta/2+it_2$, attached to the Euclidean thermal circle. Integrals along them become the real-time integrals of the retarded ladder.

at.quote: will be called the two “left/right rails” respectively

defs.html: The time over which out-of-time-ordered correlators of a chaotic system grow from small to order one, of order $\lambda_L^{-1}\log N$ at large $N$. Beyond it they stop growing and eventually decay.

at.quote: the scrambling time of the undeformed theory

defs.html: The space of conformal theories connected by exactly marginal deformations, with the marginal couplings as coordinates. A line of fixed points is a one-dimensional example; the paper's supersymmetric models have conformal manifolds of very large dimension.

at.quote: it has a conformal manifold even at finite

defs.html: Conformal SYK, the model of Gross and Rosenhaus: $N$ generalized free fermions of dimension $1/q$ in $0+1$ dimensions, coupled by an SYK interaction. That interaction is then classically marginal and argued to be exactly marginal at leading order in $1/N$.

at.quote: One is the cSYK line of fixed points

defs.html: An argument that a supersymmetric theory has a conformal manifold when the conditions for vanishing beta functions, which in supersymmetric theories are conditions on anomalous dimensions, are fewer than the couplings. The solutions then form a family of fixed points.

at.quote: Using the Leigh-Strassler argument

defs.html: The ring of chiral primary operators of a supersymmetric theory, with their non-singular product. In $1+1$d $\mathcal N=(2,2)$ theories a chiral primary of R-charge $r$ has dimension $r/2$, so the chiral primaries of R-charge 2 give the marginal deformations.

at.quote: the generating function of the chiral ring

questions.q: What do $J$, $q$, $\Delta$ and $\beta$ mean, and which end of the line is which?
questions.a: $N$ copies of a core CFT are coupled by products of $q$ operators, each of dimension $\Delta$, with Gaussian random couplings of variance set by $J^2$. Exact marginality needs $\Delta=1/q$ in the examples. $J=0$ is $N$ decoupled copies; $J\to\infty$ is usually an SYK-like fixed point. The paper sets $\beta=2\pi$, so the chaos bound reads $\lambda_L\le1$.

questions.q: Why insist on exactly marginal disorder?
questions.a: The ladder method for $\lambda_L$ needs conformal eigenfunctions, so it works only in a conformal theory. With relevant disorder that holds only at the infrared endpoint, which gives a single value of $\lambda_L$. With exactly marginal disorder every $J$ is a conformal theory, so $\lambda_L(J)$ can be followed continuously from $J=0$.

questions.q: If the equations need every correlator of the core CFT, are they useful?
questions.a: Solving them exactly needs every correlator, so it is possible only for special core theories, here generalized free fields. But to a given order in $J$ only finitely many correlators enter, so perturbation theory in $J$ is always possible. That is how the minimal model is treated, at leading order, where only its four-point function is needed.

questions.q: Why does the chaos analysis stay in $0+1$ and $1+1$ dimensions?
questions.a: The double commutator is a continuation of thermal four-point functions on a cylinder. In $0+1$ and $1+1$ dimensions these are conformal maps of flat-space correlators, which the ladder of section 2 computes; in higher dimensions they are not, so the flat-space ladder does not directly give the thermal one.

questions.q: What is $\lambda_L^0$, and why is it not the chaos exponent of one copy?
questions.a: It is the exponent of the double commutator of a single undeformed copy at very late times, beyond its scrambling time. There the commutator no longer grows but decays, as unitarity requires, so $\lambda_L^0$ is expected to be zero or negative even when the copy is chaotic. For the generalized free fields it is $-2\Delta$, for the $A_2$ minimal model 0.

questions.q: Why is a negative root of $k_R=1$ read as zero chaos?
questions.a: The method keeps only exponentially growing pieces of the double commutator, so a negative exponent is not self-consistent: terms that were dropped can be larger. But if the largest root is negative, there is no positive one, which the method would have found. So nothing grows exponentially, and the paper takes the physical exponent to be $\max(0,\lambda_L)$.

questions.q: In what sense is the transition discontinuous?
questions.a: In the paper's sense, chaos is absent for every coupling below a finite $J_c$ and present above it, so it does not grow from $J=0$. The plotted exponent itself rises from zero at $J_c$, without a jump. The contrast is with the continuous case, where any small coupling already gives a small positive exponent.

questions.q: How close is the analogy with the KAM theorem?
questions.a: Only loose, as the paper says: the analogy is far from precise. In both cases a system deformed from a non-chaotic point needs a finite deformation before chaos appears. But KAM concerns classical systems with finitely many degrees of freedom and invariant tori, while here the systems are large-$N$ quantum field theories and chaos is measured by $\lambda_L$.

questions.q: Why do generalized free fields and the minimal model behave differently?
questions.a: By the continuity relation, the weak-coupling exponent is the late-time exponent of one copy. For generalized free fields the double commutator of one copy decays as $e^{-2\Delta t}$, so $\lambda_L$ starts negative and chaos needs a finite coupling. For the $A_2$ minimal model it tends to a constant, so $\lambda_L$ starts at zero and chaos can grow from $J=0$.

questions.q: How can minimal models turn into generalized free fields?
questions.a: Average $N_f$ copies of the chiral field into $\Psi=\sum_a\Phi_a/\sqrt{N_f}$. In its four-point function the Wick-like pairings come with weight one, while the connected part of the single-copy correlator is suppressed by $1/N_f$, and likewise at higher points. So at large $N_f$ the field is generalized free, and the minimal models' conformal manifold becomes theirs.

questions.q: What does the paper not show?
questions.a: The continuity relation is argued and checked in two families, not proved. For the minimal model only $q=3$ and the leading order in $J$ are computed; that $\lambda_L$ then grows with $J$ is assumed, and the higher-order argument omits the Euclidean integrals. The bosonic kernel is assumed to dominate. cSYK's marginality holds only at leading order in $1/N$.

questions.q: Which other theories should show a discontinuous onset?
questions.a: If the continuity relation holds generally, any core CFT whose late-time exponent $\lambda_L^0$ is negative should give one, provided a conformal manifold can be built from it at large $N$. On the basis of known late-time behaviour, the paper expects this for the non-supersymmetric minimal models and the $2+1$d Ising model, if such conformal manifolds exist.

questions.q: What does the chaos exponent measure?
questions.a: How quickly a small perturbation spreads through a quantum system. One perturbs with an operator at time zero and asks how much it fails to commute with another operator at time $t$. In a chaotic many-body system the squared commutator grows as $e^{\lambda_Lt}$ until it saturates, and $\lambda_L$ plays the role of a classical Lyapunov exponent.
